title: Equipotential Bonding: 7 Essential Rules for Safer Plants
text:
Electrical Safety & Standards

 Equipotential Bonding: 7 Essential Rules for Safer Plants

 A person touching a water pipe and a faulty appliance at the same time can be exposed to a dangerous voltage difference, even when the earthing looks perfect. Good bonding joins all touchable metalwork so that difference stays too small to hurt anyone.

 
 Main Bonding 
 Supplementary Bonding 
 Extraneous Parts 
 IEC 60364 
 Continuity Tests 
 




 Earthing gives fault current a path, but it does not by itself keep nearby metal parts at the same voltage. Equipotential bonding closes that gap by joining pipes, steelwork and equipment frames with properly sized conductors.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn what equipotential bonding is, how main and supplementary bonding conductors are sized and tested, and where IEC 60364 and IS 732 demand them.


 
 
 
 What Is Equipotential Bonding?


 Equipotential bonding is the practice of connecting all exposed conductive parts and extraneous conductive parts in an installation with low resistance conductors, so that they rise and fall in voltage together during a fault. It works alongside the earthing arrangement described in TN, TT and IT earthing systems , and it is the main reason touch voltages stay safe while a protective device clears the fault.


 An exposed conductive part is the metal body of equipment, such as a motor frame, which becomes live only under fault. An extraneous conductive part is metal outside the installation that can introduce a potential, such as a water pipe, gas line or structural steel.


 
 
 
 

 Image credit: Electrical Engineering Portal . Photo courtesy of Electrical Engineering Portal, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 The photo shows an equipotential busbar, where bonding conductors from services and steelwork meet the main earthing terminal. Without it, a fault can leave a pipe at a very different voltage from the frame beside it, a classic cause of electric shock in plant rooms.


 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Why Bonding Matters Even With Good Earthing


 When a phase conductor touches a metal enclosure, fault current flows through the protective conductor and develops a voltage across it. A good earth electrode, sized as shown in earthing resistance calculation , does not remove this voltage, it only sets how much current flows back to the source.


 If a nearby water pipe is still at true earth potential, a person holding both the pipe and the enclosure sees the full voltage drop on the protective conductor. Equipotential bonding pulls the pipe up to the same voltage as the frame, so the hand to hand voltage becomes small.

 Do You Know?
 Substation earth grids use the same idea on a larger scale, with a buried mesh acting as equipotential bonding for the whole switchyard. IEEE 80 calls the resulting limits step and touch voltage.



 Types of Equipotential Bonding in an Installation


 
 Main Protective Bonding
 Joins incoming metal services and building steel to the main earthing terminal near their point of entry.
 Best for: every building and plant substation
 Mandatory 

 Supplementary Bonding
 Joins exposed and extraneous parts that can be touched together in one location.
 Best for: bathrooms, plant rooms and pump houses
 Local 

 Functional Bonding
 Provides a clean reference for electronics, screens and signal circuits.
 Best for: control rooms and instrument panels
 Signal 

 Lightning and Static Bonding
 Joins metal parts to stop flashover and spark discharge.
 Best for: tank farms, roof steel and hazardous areas
 Protective 




 Main and supplementary equipotential bonding protect people from shock. Functional bonding for instruments follows the rules in grounding techniques and earthing in process plants , yet all of them meet at one earthing system.


 IEC, IS and BS Rules for Equipotential Bonding


 
 
 Standard What It Covers Key Requirement 

 IEC 60364 4 41 Protection against electric shock Main bonding in every building, supplementary bonding where disconnection is not fast enough 

 IEC 60364 5 54 Earthing arrangements and protective conductors Conductor sizes for main and supplementary bonding 

 IS 732 Indian code for wiring installations Follows the IEC 60364 approach for bonding 

 IS 3043 Indian code of practice for earthing Earth electrodes, earthing conductors and bonding of metalwork 

 BS 7671 UK wiring regulations Clause 544 for bonding sizes and connection points 

 IEC 60079 14 Electrical installations in hazardous areas Potential equalisation of all exposed and extraneous parts 

 



 Quick Tip
 Before you size anything, ask which earthing system the site uses, because the bonding conductor size is linked to the main earthing conductor. A TN C S supply in a city building and a TT supply on a remote pump site lead to different numbers.



 Equipotential Bonding Conductor Sizes and Formula


 Electrical Engineering Portal, quoting IEC 60364 5 54, gives 6 mm² copper as the minimum main bonding conductor and notes that copper need not exceed 25 mm². The same article lists 2.5 mm² copper for supplementary bonding with mechanical protection and 4 mm² copper without it.


 IEC 60364 5 54 also requires the main bonding conductor to be at least half the cross section of the largest protective earthing conductor, with 16 mm² aluminium or 50 mm² steel as alternatives to 6 mm² copper. For the effectiveness of supplementary equipotential bonding, IEC 60364 4 41 gives the resistance check shown below.


 
 Main bonding size S ≥ 0.5 × S earthing conductor, minimum 6 mm² copper, need not exceed 25 mm² copper 
 Supplementary bonding: R ≤ 50 V ÷ Ia for AC, R ≤ 120 V ÷ Ia for DC
